_provenance: Taxonomy, standards facts and technology names derive from three architecture reviews synthesised in the harness composition deck, current to approximately mid-2026. Enterprise ownership and build phases are architectural recommendations, not findings. Re-verify all version-specific and statistical claims before publication.

buildPhases.blurb: Real systems, real data, real users.

buildPhases.name: Phase 3 · Scale & federation

modelCore.name: Models
modelCore.mandate: The models themselves: the generative and representational capability every harness exists to make safe, grounded, affordable and accountable. Everything outside this circle is the harness.
owns: Large language models and vision-language models for reasoning and generation
Speech models (ASR / TTS) for voice channels
Embedding and reranking models behind retrieval
A deliberate mix of proprietary and open-weight models, kept swappable

down.why: served and versioned by the inference harness

oss: Open-weight families served locally (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma)
standards: OpenAI-compatible chat/completions APIs as the de facto wire format
modelCore.deptAcc: AI Engineering, with model selection reviewed by Architecture and Risk
roles: Model evaluation lead — chooses and re-chooses models on evidence
Applied scientist — prompt and structured-output design
Procurement / vendor manager — commercial terms, data-use clauses
modelCore.phaseNote: Start with one strong hosted model plus one open-weight fallback. Pin versions from day one: silent upgrades break prompts.
risks: Model swaps silently change behaviour when versions are not pinned
Capability assumed rather than measured on your own tasks
Vendor terms that permit training on your prompts
signals: Task success on your own eval set, not public benchmarks
Cost and latency per successful task by model
Share of traffic on open-weight fallback (portability test)
modelCore.note: The core is deliberately thin. Reasoning quality is only one input to a working system: the sixteen rings around it decide whether that reasoning is grounded, permitted, observable and worth its cost.

1.name: Infrastructure & Runtime
1.mandate: The compute, scheduling, networking and resilience substrate every other harness sits on — Kubernetes across public and private cloud, GPU-aware and multi-tenant from the start.
owns: Kubernetes clusters across public and private cloud, with a private path for regulated workloads
GPU scheduling, quota and gang-scheduling so accelerators are not idle
Storage, queues, service mesh, secrets distribution and network policy
High availability, disaster recovery and capacity planning
Tenancy primitives: namespaces, node pools, network segmentation

down.why: GPU pools and autoscaling for inference
durable execution needs stateful backing services

cross.why: network policy, secrets, workload identity roots

roles: Head of Platform Engineering — accountable owner
Site reliability engineer — SLOs, capacity, DR drills
Kubernetes platform engineer — cluster and GPU scheduling
Network and infrastructure security engineer
FinOps analyst — accelerator cost per team
1.phaseNote: Done when a team can deploy an agent workload to a private-cloud cluster with GPU quota, secrets, a network policy and a tested restore — without filing a ticket.
risks: GPU utilisation stuck at 25–35% without quota and gang scheduling; disciplined scheduling moves it to roughly 60–85%
Noisy-neighbour effects across tenants sharing accelerators
Cold starts on scale-from-zero making interactive agents feel broken
Disaster recovery documented but never rehearsed
signals: GPU utilisation and queue wait time
Scale-from-zero cold start P95
Cluster availability against SLO
Cost per GPU hour by tenant
Restore time in the last DR drill
1.note: Two things commonly hide inside Infrastructure and should not: model serving and the AI gateway. Both have their own lifecycle and trust boundary, which is why they are separate harnesses here.

2.name: Model & Inference
2.mandate: Serve, version and scale the models — proprietary and open-weight — with predictable latency and cost, and keep them swappable so no single provider becomes load-bearing.
owns: Inference serving: batching, KV cache, tensor and pipeline parallelism
Model registry and version pinning, including deprecation calendars
Routing between model tiers, plus fallbacks when a provider degrades
Embedding and reranking endpoints used by retrieval
Capacity and quota per tenant on shared accelerators

cross.why: consumes assembled context under a token budget
model changes gated by regression evaluation

managed: Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry
standards: Model cards for each served version
roles: Head of ML Platform — accountable owner
Inference engineer — serving performance and memory
GPU performance engineer — batching, quantisation, cache
Model operations engineer — versions, rollouts, deprecations
2.phaseNote: Pilot needs one hosted model and one self-hosted fallback behind the same interface, both version-pinned, with a documented switch procedure.
risks: Vendor lock-in through provider-specific features in prompts and tools
Silent provider upgrades shifting behaviour mid-quarter
KV cache reuse leaking context across tenants if isolation is careless
P99 latency collapsing under burst without admission control
signals: Time to first token and tokens per second
P99 end-to-end latency by model tier
Prefix cache hit rate
Cost per thousand tokens by tenant
Share of traffic that could fail over to the open-weight path
2.note: Keeping this harness distinct from Infrastructure is what makes model choice reversible. If serving is buried in the platform, changing models becomes a platform migration.

3.name: AI Gateway
3.mandate: One control point for every model call: authentication, tenant quota, routing, caching, cost metering and the edge layer of guardrail enforcement.
owns: Authentication and authorisation for callers, human and agent
Per-tenant quotas, rate limits and budget ceilings
Semantic and cost-aware routing across model tiers and providers
Response and prefix caching
Token metering and chargeback per team, tenant and task
Edge guardrail hooks: request and response screening before anything reaches a model

up.why: applies guardrail policy at the edge

managed: Cloud API gateways with AI plugins
Commercial LLM gateways with observability bundled
3.deptAcc: Platform Engineering, with Identity & Access Management
roles: Platform engineering lead — accountable owner
API gateway engineer — routing, caching, rate limits
IAM engineer — token issuance, scopes, workload identity
FinOps analyst — budgets and chargeback
3.phaseNote: Pilot needs authentication, per-tenant quota and token metering. Semantic routing and caching are optimisations for phase 2.
risks: A single point of failure for every agent in the estate
P99 spikes above roughly 500 requests per second on a single gateway process — shard horizontally
Policy drift between gateway guardrails and the in-loop guardrails, so a call blocked at one layer passes at the other
Cache keys that ignore tenant, leaking responses across boundaries
signals: Requests per second and gateway-added P99 overhead
Quota and budget rejections by tenant
Cache hit rate and cache-attributable savings
Cost per tenant per day against budget
3.note: Splitting the gateway out of Infrastructure was one of two structural corrections to the original ten-harness model. It is the only place where cost, identity and routing can be governed for every call at once.

4.name: Experience & Interaction
4.mandate: The surfaces where people meet the system — and where they steer it: channels, streaming, sessions, clarification, provenance display and the approval moments that make autonomy safe.
owns: Channels: web, mobile, chat platforms, voice and public API
Streaming and partial-result rendering so long tasks stay legible
Session and conversation state at the edge
Clarification prompts when the task is under-specified
Approval and review surfaces for human-in-the-loop checkpoints
Provenance display: what the answer was based on and how confident it is
Multimodal input and output, and accessibility

down.why: every request enters through the gateway

cross.why: renders approval checkpoints and autonomy state
shows source and lineage behind answers

managed: Enterprise chat platforms (Teams, Slack) as channels
standards: Art. 50 EU AI Act disclosure for machine interaction
4.deptAcc: Product Engineering / Digital Channels, with UX
roles: Product lead — accountable owner
Frontend engineer — streaming, sessions, channel adapters
UX designer — approval, clarification and provenance patterns
Content designer — the words in the interface
Accessibility specialist
4.phaseNote: Pilot can ship one channel with streaming. Approval and clarification surfaces become mandatory the moment agents can write to production systems.
risks: No clarification path, so the agent invents assumptions instead of asking
Approval fatigue: too many low-stakes confirmations and reviewers stop reading
Provenance hidden, so users cannot calibrate trust
Disclosure obligations missed for chatbots regardless of risk tier
signals: Task completion and abandonment rate
Clarification rate and its effect on success
Approval latency and reviewer override rate
Accessibility conformance
User-reported trust or satisfaction
4.note: This is the harness most often skipped in an architecture diagram and most often blamed in a post-mortem. Autonomy policy is only real if there is a surface where a human can actually intervene in time.

5.name: Domain & Semantic
5.mandate: Shared, machine-usable meaning: ontologies, a semantic layer, agreed metric definitions and regulation expressed as knowledge the agent can reason over.
owns: Domain ontology and taxonomy — entities, relationships, business rules
Semantic layer and metric definitions so one term returns one number
Glossary and synonym mapping between business and system vocabulary
Regulation as knowledge: rules the agent must understand, distinct from policy it must obey
Stewardship: who owns each definition and how changes are reviewed

up.why: definitions bind to physical data through contracts

cross.why: feature and metric definitions shared with classical models

oss: RDF, OWL, SKOS and SHACL shapes
Neo4j or an RDF triple store
managed: Catalog products with a governed business glossary
standards: Open Semantic Interchange (OSI) alignment for metric definitions
5.deptAcc: Data Governance / Enterprise Architecture, with domain SMEs
roles: Chief Data Officer or Head of Data Governance — accountable owner
Ontologist / taxonomist — models the domain
Data steward per domain — owns definitions and approves changes
Domain subject-matter expert — supplies the ground truth
Semantic engineer — implements and tests the layer
5.phaseNote: Start with the twenty terms that appear in disputed answers, not a full enterprise ontology. Expand only where ambiguity has actually cost something.
risks: Semantic drift: definitions diverge quietly between teams and the agent answers confidently from the wrong one
An ontology nobody owns after the consultants leave
Regulation held only as prose, so nothing downstream can act on it
Modelling the whole enterprise before proving value on one domain
signals: Coverage of disputed terms with an approved definition
Definition change rate and steward review time
Metric disagreement incidents per quarter
Share of agent answers traceable to a governed definition
5.note: This harness is what stops a competent-sounding agent from being subtly wrong about your business. It is also the slowest to build, which is why it belongs in phase 2 rather than the pilot.

6.name: Data Integration & Provenance
6.q: Where does enterprise truth come from?
6.mandate: Governed access to source systems with lineage and entitlements attached — the data plane behind retrieval, deliberately separate from the tool plane that takes actions.
owns: Connectors and data servers exposing systems of record to agents
Data contracts: schema, freshness and quality guarantees per source
Lineage from source through transformation to the answer
Entitlements: row and column security carried through to the agent
Federated query across warehouses, lakes and operational stores
Classification of sensitive fields before anything is indexed

up.why: binds physical data to agreed definitions

down.why: supplies the corpus retrieval draws on

cross.why: lineage feeds audit and incident replay

oss: Apache Ranger or OPA for row and column policy
managed: Enterprise MCP data servers from vendors
standards: MCP for exposing data to agents
6.deptAcc: Data Engineering, with Data Governance and Privacy
roles: Head of Data Engineering — accountable owner
Data engineer — connectors, contracts, pipelines
Data steward — source ownership and quality
Privacy officer — classification, minimisation, retention
Security engineer — entitlement propagation
6.phaseNote: Connect three sources properly — contract, lineage, entitlements — before connecting thirty carelessly. MCP data servers shorten integration work substantially, but the governance is the slow part, not the plumbing.
risks: The agent inherits broader entitlements than the human it acts for
PII copied into vector indexes where deletion obligations cannot be met
Stale or silently broken sources answering confidently
No lineage, so an incorrect answer cannot be traced to its source
signals: Freshness against contract per source
Contract test pass rate
Entitlement violations detected (target zero)
Lineage coverage as a share of answers
Time to honour a deletion request across indexes
6.note: Data access and tool execution are different trust boundaries. Reading a governed table and calling an API that moves money should never share one permission model — that separation is why this harness exists apart from Tool, Skill & Sandbox.

7.name: Retrieval & Context Engineering
7.mandate: Assemble the smallest sufficient context for each step, inside a token budget: hybrid retrieval, reranking, graph traversal, iterative refinement, compaction and tool search.
owns: Hybrid retrieval (lexical plus dense) with reranking
GraphRAG and structured retrieval where relationships matter
Agentic, iterative retrieval that refines its own queries
Context pruning and compaction to fight bloat
Token budgeting per step and per task
Tool search: retrieving relevant tool definitions instead of loading all of them

down.why: delivers the assembled context to the model

cross.why: context tokens are a first-class cost

managed: Managed vector and hybrid search services
standards: MCP tool-search patterns for tool-definition retrieval
Structured citation formats carried into answers
roles: Head of AI Engineering — accountable owner
Retrieval / information-retrieval engineer
Context engineer — budgets, compaction, prompt assembly
ML engineer — embedding and reranker selection
Data engineer — indexing pipelines and freshness
7.phaseNote: Pilot ships hybrid retrieval with reranking and a hard token budget. Add graph retrieval and iterative refinement once you can measure groundedness.
risks: Context bloat and lost-in-the-middle: more context, worse answers, higher cost
Retrieval poisoning — hostile content in the corpus becomes instructions
Tool definitions consuming the context window; tool search cuts that overhead by roughly 85%
Index staleness invisible to the user
signals: Recall at k and reranker gain
Groundedness and citation accuracy
Context tokens per successful task
Retrieval latency P95
Share of answers with a verifiable source
7.note: Retrieval, memory and runtime state are three different things. Retrieval is what the system looks up now; memory is what it chose to keep; runtime state is where the task currently stands. Merging them is a common and expensive modelling error.

8.name: Memory & State
8.mandate: Decide deliberately what persists beyond a task — working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory — with an explicit write policy, retention limits and poisoning controls.
owns: Working memory within a task and session
Episodic memory: what happened before, per user and per tenant
Semantic memory: durable facts learned about the domain and the user
Procedural memory: how this organisation does a task
Write policy — what earns a place in memory — plus TTL and forgetting
Redaction, tenant partitioning and the right to erasure

up.why: task state and checkpoints coordinate with memory

down.why: recall is merged into assembled context

managed: Managed vector stores with tenancy controls
Agent platforms with built-in memory services
standards: CoALA as the reference model for memory types
roles: Head of AI Engineering — accountable owner
ML engineer — recall quality and write policy
Backend engineer — stores, partitioning, TTL enforcement
Data privacy officer — retention, erasure, minimisation
8.phaseNote: Pilot may use session-scoped memory only. Long-lived cross-session memory should not ship before poisoning controls and erasure both work.
risks: Memory poisoning: a hostile fact written once and trusted forever (OWASP ASI06)
Unbounded growth degrading recall precision and cost
Cross-tenant leakage through a shared store or a careless key
A wrong memory causing the same error repeatedly, with confidence
Erasure requests that cannot be honoured across derived indexes
signals: Recall usefulness — memory hits that improved the outcome
Write rate and store growth per tenant
TTL adherence and orphaned record count
Cross-tenant assertions (target zero)
Erasure completion time
8.note: Memory is where an agent stops being stateless and starts accumulating liability. A write policy is a governance artefact, not an implementation detail.

9.name: Protocol & Interoperability
9.q: How do agents, tools and peers talk?
9.mandate: Standard contracts at every boundary so frameworks stay replaceable: MCP downward to tools and data, A2A sideways to peer agents, OpenAPI and AsyncAPI to the rest of the estate.
owns: MCP servers and clients for tools, resources and prompts
A2A agent cards, task lifecycle and artifacts for agent-to-agent work
OpenAPI and AsyncAPI contracts for conventional services and events
Registries: which agents, tools and skills exist, at which version, owned by whom
Version and deprecation policy across protocol revisions
Supply-chain scanning of third-party servers and skills

up.why: tools are exposed as typed contracts

cross.why: scanning, signing and pinning of servers and skills

oss: mcp-scan for server and tool scanning
A2A SDKs (five languages under the Linux Foundation)
managed: Vendor MCP servers for major SaaS systems
standards: MCP revision 2025-11-25; stateless core 2026-07-28 (Dynamic Client Registration replaced by Client ID Metadata Documents; Roots, Sampling and Logging deprecated)
A2A v1.0 under the Linux Foundation / AAIF, 150+ organisations
Agent Skills open standard (SKILL.md), published December 2025
roles: Chief or enterprise architect — accountable owner
Integration architect — boundary contracts and versioning
API product manager — registry, lifecycle, deprecation
Security architect — supply chain and protocol threat model
9.phaseNote: Adopt MCP in the pilot to avoid rewriting integrations later. A2A federation and a shared agent registry are the phase 3 workstream, once more than one team runs agents that must delegate to each other.
risks: Tool poisoning, rug-pulls and tool shadowing from third-party servers
Version skew as the MCP stateless core lands and deprecated features are removed
Registry sprawl: nobody knows how many agents exist
Insecure inter-agent communication (OWASP ASI07) once A2A is in play
signals: Share of integrations on standard contracts rather than bespoke glue
Schema-break incidents per quarter
Registry coverage against deployed reality
Scan findings on third-party servers and skills, and time to remediate
9.note: Frameworks turn over every few quarters; protocols outlive them. Being protocol-centric rather than framework-centric is the single decision that most reduces future rework.

10.name: Orchestration & Durable Execution
10.q: Who acts, when and in what order?
10.mandate: Plan and decompose the task, route work to the right agent or tool, checkpoint durably so long tasks survive restarts, and stop cleanly when budget or policy says so.
owns: Planning and decomposition; orchestrator-worker and handoff patterns
Durable checkpoints, retries and idempotency for side-effecting steps
Termination policy: step limits, budget ceilings, loop detection
State machines that make agent behaviour inspectable
Multi-agent topology decisions, including when not to use one
Resumption after human approval without replaying side effects

up.why: only cleared requests enter the loop

down.why: writes back what is worth keeping

oss: Microsoft Agent Framework (Semantic Kernel plus AutoGen)
Airflow or Dagster for batch paths
standards: A2A task lifecycle for delegated work
Idempotency keys on all side-effecting calls
OpenTelemetry span conventions for agent runs
roles: Principal agent architect — accountable owner
Agent engineer — patterns, planners, handoffs
Distributed systems engineer — durability, retries, idempotency
SRE — termination policy, circuit breakers, on-call
10.phaseNote: Pilot needs a single orchestrator with durable checkpoints and a hard step and budget ceiling. Multi-agent topologies only after a single agent has been measured and found insufficient.
risks: Infinite loops and runaway token spend without termination policy
Non-idempotent retries producing duplicate real-world side effects
Multi-agent architectures used by default: roughly 15× the tokens of a single chat turn, with token use explaining about 80% of performance variance
Token duplication across agents (one framework measured at 72%) and plan-and-execute patterns cutting spend by around 83%
Long tasks losing all progress on a restart
signals: Task success rate and steps per successful task
Token cost per successful task, not per call
Circuit-breaker and termination trips
Checkpoint recovery success rate
Share of tasks resumed correctly after approval
10.note: Parallel exploration is worth roughly 15× the tokens only when the work genuinely fans out. Gate multi-agent expansion on measured return, not on architectural fashion.

11.name: Tool, Skill & Sandbox
11.q: What can the system actually do?
11.mandate: The action surface: typed tool contracts, packaged skills, an explicit read-versus-write authority model, and isolation strong enough for code the model wrote.
owns: Tool contracts with typed inputs, outputs and error semantics
Skills as packaged, versioned capability (SKILL.md and equivalents)
Read-versus-write authority classification for every tool
Sandboxing for generated code and untrusted execution
Idempotency, dry-run and rollback for side-effecting tools
Tool catalogue, ownership and deprecation

up.why: write actions require the approval gate

oss: WebAssembly runtimes such as Wasmtime (under 5 ms start, weaker native library support)
managed: Vendor tool catalogues and connector suites
standards: Default-deny egress, ephemeral filesystem, no host secrets in the sandbox
11.deptAcc: AI Engineering, with Security Engineering co-signing write authority
roles: Head of AI Engineering — accountable owner
Tool platform engineer — contracts, catalogue, versioning
Application security engineer — sandbox posture and review
SRE — blast radius, rate limits, rollback
Business system owner — approves write access to their system
11.phaseNote: Ship read-only tools in the pilot. Every write tool should arrive with an approval path, an idempotency key and a rollback story — no exceptions in phase 2.
risks: Excessive agency: broad write scopes granted for convenience
Supply-chain risk in third-party skills — one audit found roughly 36% flawed and 76 outright malicious
Sandbox escape, or no sandbox at all for generated code
Side effects repeated on retry because idempotency was never designed in
Tool descriptions themselves acting as an injection vector
signals: Tool error and timeout rate by tool
Share of write tools behind an approval gate (target 100%)
Blocked unsigned or unscanned tool loads
Sandbox escape attempts detected
Rollback success rate for reversed actions
11.note: Sandbox choice is a real trade-off: microVMs give the strongest isolation at around 125–150 ms of start latency, WebAssembly starts in under 5 ms but constrains native libraries. Pick per tool class, not once for the platform.

12.name: ML & Decision Intelligence
12.q: When is a classical model the better tool?
12.mandate: Keep discriminative and optimisation models in the architecture as first-class tools and routing signals — often cheaper, faster and more accurate than asking a language model.
owns: Classifiers for routing, triage, intent and safety pre-screening
Rerankers and scorers supporting retrieval
Anomaly detection and forecasting feeding agent decisions
Optimisation and constraint solving where the answer is a plan, not prose
Feature store, training pipelines and drift monitoring for these models

down.why: routing signals for model tier selection

cross.why: held to the same evaluation discipline

managed: Managed ML platforms and feature stores
standards: Existing model-risk management standards where the sector requires them
roles: Head of Data Science — accountable owner
Data scientist — model development and validation
MLOps engineer — deployment, monitoring, retraining
Decision scientist — where optimisation beats generation
Model risk reviewer in regulated sectors
12.phaseNote: A scale-phase optimisation: introduce when volume makes a measured LLM path too slow, too costly or too imprecise for a repeated decision. Do not create a parallel ML organisation — reuse the same registry, evaluation and observability harnesses.
risks: A language model used where a small classifier is faster, cheaper and more accurate
Drift unmonitored because these models sit outside the agent telemetry
Two disconnected lifecycles: one for models, one for agents
Existing model-risk governance not applied to models now invoked by agents
signals: Accuracy or AUC by model against its baseline
Feature and prediction drift
Share of decisions served by classical models versus the LLM path
Cost and latency delta against the LLM alternative
12.note: This harness is easy to forget in an agent-centric design and quick to pay for itself. The most reliable cost reduction available is usually not a cheaper model tier — it is not calling a language model at all.

13.name: Security, Safety & Guardrails
13.q: Who or what is allowed to do it?
13.mandate: Runtime enforcement on every call, plus the agentic attack surface: non-human identity, injection and PII defence, output validation, supply chain, circuit breakers and kill switches.
owns: Deterministic checks pre-call, in-loop and post-call
Prompt-injection and jailbreak defence, including on retrieved content
PII and PHI detection and redaction in both directions
Output validation against schema and policy before anything executes
Non-human identity: one identity per agent, tool and server; just-in-time scoping
Supply-chain controls: signing, scanning, pinning, SBOM and AIBOM
Circuit breakers and kill switches with a tested revocation path

up.why: policy is authored in governance and enforced here

managed: Commercial AI security posture and runtime protection platforms
standards: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI01 goal hijack, ASI03 identity and privilege abuse, ASI04 supply chain, ASI06 memory and context poisoning, ASI07 insecure inter-agent communication, ASI10 rogue agents
NIST SP 800-207 zero trust, applied to non-human identity
roles: CISO — accountable owner
Application security engineer — guardrails and validation
IAM architect — non-human identity and just-in-time scoping
Red team — adversarial testing against the deployed system
Privacy engineer — detection, redaction, minimisation
Incident responder — agent-specific runbooks
13.phaseNote: Pilot needs injection screening, PII redaction, output validation and workload identity. Full supply-chain control and inter-agent security are mandatory before production data or write access.
risks: Prompt injection arriving through retrieved documents, tool descriptions or peer agents rather than the user
Static API keys standing in for agent identity
Guardrails only at the edge, so anything inside the loop is unprotected
An agent able to do more than the human it acts for
Third-party MCP servers and skills trusted without scanning or pinning
signals: Attack success rate, always published with the harness and judge configuration
Injection attempts detected and blocked
Coverage of just-in-time credentials versus static keys
Unsigned or unscanned artefact loads blocked
Mean time to detect and to revoke a misbehaving agent
13.note: Guardrails and governance are different jobs: guardrails enforce on every call, governance decides what the rules are and who may waive them. Keeping them distinct but linked is what stops policy from becoming decorative.

14.name: Governance, Oversight & AgentOps
14.q: What autonomy is allowed, and how does it evolve?
14.mandate: Decide how much independence each action may have, prove it with policy-as-code and human checkpoints, and run the change control that lets the system improve safely.
owns: Risk-based autonomy tiers: autonomy level as a function of action impact, uncertainty, identity, data sensitivity, regulation, reversibility and confidence
Human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop checkpoints at durable pause points
Policy-as-code compiled into gateway and runtime enforcement
Registries for agents, prompts, models, tools, skills, datasets and policies
CI/CD, canary and shadow release, with rollback
Audit trail, lineage and evidence packs for regulators
Feedback capture flowing into fine-tuning, distillation and prompt change
Incident process and post-incident change
oss: Backstage as a service and agent catalogue
Temporal for approvals as durable steps
DataHub or OpenMetadata for audit lineage
managed: GRC platforms with AI control mappings
Model and agent registries from cloud vendors
standards: NIST AI Risk Management Framework plus the Generative AI Profile (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage)

EU AI Act — general application from 2 August 2026; Art. 50 transparency duties apply to any chatbot or generated content regardless of risk tier; Annex III high-risk obligations deferred to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus of 27 July 2026
Sector regulation and internal model-risk policy
14.deptAcc: AI Governance Office / Risk & Compliance, with Legal
roles: Chief Risk or Compliance Officer, or Head of Responsible AI — accountable owner
AI risk manager — autonomy tiers and control design
Compliance analyst — framework mapping and evidence
Legal counsel — regulatory interpretation and contracts
Product owner — accepts residual risk for their agent
Internal audit — independent assurance
Release manager — gates, canaries, rollback
14.phaseNote: Keep it lightweight in the pilot: an agent registry, an owner per agent and a written autonomy tier. Promote to full control the moment agents touch production systems or personal data — before any traffic, not after.
risks: Approval theatre: reviewers who cannot see enough context to disagree
Policy drift between the written standard and the deployed rules
Shadow agents outside any registry
Transparency obligations missed because the system was classified as low risk
Feedback captured but never reaching a model or prompt change
signals: Share of actions executed inside the policy envelope
Approval latency and override rate
Registry completeness against deployed reality
Control coverage mapped to the chosen framework
Time to revoke or roll back an agent
Share of incidents that produced a durable change
14.note: Autonomy is a policy, not a switch. The formula above lets one system be fully autonomous for reversible reads and strictly gated for irreversible writes, which is the only configuration that survives contact with a regulated environment.

15.name: Observability & FinOps
15.q: What happened — and what did it cost?
15.mandate: Make any task reconstructable end to end and attribute its cost: OpenTelemetry GenAI spans carrying trace, thread and task IDs, the acting identity, the policy decision and the token spend.
owns: Distributed tracing across model calls, tool executions, retrieval, memory and agent runs
Correlation IDs that survive handoffs, queues and human approvals
Time-travel debugging: replay of prompts, delegations and memory state at failure
Quality and drift monitoring, including silent-failure detection
Token metering, budgets, chargeback and cost per successful task
Agent-versus-human attribution in every log
standards: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (around v1.41; agent-orchestration and MCP-tool spans still draft — design correlation IDs that survive the spec settling)
roles: Head of SRE — accountable owner
Observability engineer — instrumentation and conventions
SRE — SLOs, alerting, on-call for agent estates
FinOps analyst — budgets, chargeback, unit economics
Data engineer — trace pipelines and retention
15.phaseNote: Instrument from the first pilot request. Retrofitting correlation IDs after the fact is the most common and most expensive omission in this whole composition.
risks: Classic APM is blind to the failures that matter here: infinite loops, hallucinated queries, silent quality decay
Roughly 47% of deployed agents are actively monitored; about 68% of organisations cannot distinguish agent from human activity in their logs
Missing correlation IDs, so an incident cannot be replayed or turned into a test
Token spend discovered at the invoice rather than in the budget
signals: Trace completeness — share of tasks fully reconstructable
Share of incidents replayable from telemetry alone
Cost per successful task and budget burn rate
Agent-versus-human attribution coverage in logs
Mean time to detect a silent quality regression
15.note: OpenTelemetry is the data plane only: it records, it does not judge. Pair it with the evaluation harness or you will have perfect traces of a system nobody can say is working.

16.name: Evaluation & Assurance
16.q: Was it good, safe and compliant?
16.mandate: Grade the system at five scopes, prove reliability across repeated runs, red-team it adversarially, and gate every promotion on the evidence.
owns: Five evaluation scopes: component, agent, multi-agent trajectory, system, and trust
Trace-based grading — LLM-as-judge with calibration, agent-as-a-judge over the trajectory, human grading
N-run reliability: median, variance and cost-adjusted completion across repeated runs
Regression suites built from production incidents
Adversarial and red-team testing, including injection and harmful-action benchmarks
Shadow and canary evaluation before promotion

PH1.name: Ingress
PH1.what: Everything between the request arriving and the agent being allowed to plan. The job is to establish who is asking, on whose behalf and inside what budget — and to reject anything hostile before a single token is spent.
points: Identity is established twice: the human caller at the gateway, and the agent workload identity that will act for them
Quota and budget are cheaper to enforce before inference than to reconcile after it
Edge screening is necessary but never sufficient: retrieved content and tool output are screened again inside the loop
PH1.exit: The request is authenticated, budgeted, screened, and bound to a trace ID that follows it to the last step.

PH2.name: Agent loop
PH2.what: Plan, ground, gather, reason, gate, act — then observe the result and decide whether to go round again. The only phase that repeats, and where cost, latency and risk all accumulate.
points: The loop terminates on success, on a step or budget ceiling, or on a policy stop — never on hope
Every irreversible action passes the governance gate before execution, shown here as the alt block
State is checkpointed durably, so a restart or a wait for human approval does not lose the task
PH2.exit: Either the task is complete, or the termination policy stopped it and the partial result carries that reason.

PH3.name: Commit and egress
PH3.what: Persist what is worth keeping, validate what is about to be said, meter what it cost, and deliver it with enough provenance for the reader to judge it.

Post-call validation is the last chance to catch a schema or policy breach before the user sees it
Cost is attributed to a tenant here, which is what makes chargeback and unit economics real
PH3.exit: The user has a validated, attributable answer and the system has a durable trace of how it was produced.

PH4.name: Assurance and lifecycle
PH4.what: Not a phase in time. These exchanges run underneath every step above: telemetry becomes evaluation cases, evaluation becomes release evidence, and approved changes are redeployed into the harnesses that produced the behaviour.

Release gates consume evidence rather than opinion: N-run reliability, security scans, cost thresholds
Policy lands in two places — as enforcement in guardrails and as configuration in orchestration
PH4.exit: The system improves without anyone having to take on trust that it improved.

RUNTIME.what: Where it runs and how it is reached. In this sequence the runtime plane appears at both ends — it takes the request in and delivers the answer out — and in the middle, because every model call is routed and metered through the gateway.

KNOWLEDGE.what: What the system knows. These four lifelines are only active inside the loop: they are consulted to build context and, at the end, to decide what the task earned the right to remember.

EXECUTION.what: What the system does. Orchestration drives the whole loop; the tool, protocol and classical-model lifelines are how intent becomes an effect in the world.

TRUST.what: What keeps it accountable. Guardrails and governance interrupt the sequence; observability and evaluation run alongside it and feed the changes that alter it next time.

U.title: User or upstream system

watch: Intent captured once with no path to ask a clarifying question

watch: No clarification path, so ambiguity becomes a confident guess

does: Authenticates the caller and applies tenant quota and budget

Applies guardrail policy at the edge, both inbound and outbound

watch: An unsharded gateway becoming the estate-wide failure point

Produces schema-valid structured output

watch: Unpinned versions changing behaviour silently between releases
Structured output assumed rather than validated

CORE.role: The capability being harnessed. One exchange in forty-three — which is the point of the whole diagram.

DOM.role: Grounds the task in the organisation's own meaning before anything is retrieved.

TOOL.role: Where intent becomes effect: a typed call executed under a scoped identity inside isolation proportionate to its blast radius.

PROTO.role: Carries the call across the boundary on a standard contract, so either side can be replaced without renegotiating the integration.

MLH.role: The cheaper specialist, invoked when a classical model answers the question better than a language model.
does: Classifies, scores and routes at a fraction of the cost and latency
Detects anomalies and forecasts where the answer is a number
Solves constrained problems where the answer is a plan
MLH.contract: A tool contract like any other, with its own accuracy and drift monitoring.
watch: The LLM path used for a repeated decision a small model already answers better
Drift unmonitored because these models sit outside agent telemetry

GUARD.role: Interrupts the sequence twice — before the model and before the answer — and receives its rules from governance.
does: Screens the request for injection and sensitive data before any spend
Verifies workload identity and mints just-in-time, narrowly scoped credentials
Validates output against schema and policy, and redacts what must not leave
GUARD.contract: Cleared input with a scoped credential; schema-valid, policy-clean output or a controlled failure.
watch: Edge-only screening, when the dangerous content arrives later in retrieved documents and tool output

GOV.role: Decides how much autonomy each action gets, then closes the lifecycle loop by gating and redeploying change.

Interrupts irreversible actions for human approval at a durable checkpoint
Gates releases on evaluation evidence and redeploys versioned artefacts
Compiles policy into the rules guardrails enforce

watch: Approval theatre: reviewers without enough context to disagree
Policy drift between the written standard and the deployed rules

OBS.role: Records every hop above so the whole task can be reconstructed later. Drawn as one message; in reality it receives a span from every exchange in the diagram.

Propagates trace, thread and task IDs across handoffs and approval waits
Meters tokens and attributes cost per tenant and per task

watch: Classic APM blindness to loops, silent quality decay and hallucinated queries
Logs that cannot distinguish agent activity from human activity

EVAL.role: Turns traces into judgements, and judgements into the evidence a release gate can act on.
does: Grades component, agent, trajectory, system and trust scopes
Repeats scenarios and reports variance, not just a median
Runs adversarial campaigns and publishes attack success rate with the judge configuration
Converts production incidents into permanent regression cases
watch: Single-run scores treated as proof
Evaluation awareness inflating measured safety

EXT.title: Systems of record and peer agents
EXT.role: The world outside the harness: databases, SaaS platforms, transactional APIs, devices, and agents belonging to other teams or organisations.
does: Accepts reads and writes under the agent's scoped identity
Returns results, artifacts or long-running task handles
Applies its own authorisation — the second line of defence, not the first
EXT.contract: Whatever the system already enforces. The agent gets no special privileges.
watch: Blast radius assessed on the tool rather than on the system it touches

m1.carries: The task itself, plus the identity and entitlements of whoever is asking.
m1.contract: Authenticated channel session or API credential.
watch: Under-specified intent with no path to ask a clarifying question

m2.carries: The normalised request with session and tenant context attached.
m2.contract: Internal request envelope: tenant, session, channel, modality.
watch: Tenant inferred from the session rather than asserted explicitly

m3.carries: The request, on its way to be screened before anything is spent.
m3.contract: Synchronous guardrail call at the gateway edge, fail-closed.
watch: Fail-open behaviour when the guardrail service is slow or unavailable
Screening treated as sufficient because it happened at the edge

m4.carries: Clearance, plus a short-lived credential scoped to this task for the agent that will act.
m4.contract: Just-in-time credential bound to this task and this trace ID.
watch: Long-lived credentials issued because short-lived ones were inconvenient
Scope granted for the whole session rather than the specific action

m5.carries: The cleared task and the budget ceiling it must complete within.
m5.contract: Budget envelope plus step and termination limits, attached to the trace.
watch: A budget checked only at ingress, so an expensive loop is discovered too late

m6.carries: The planned sub-task, in whatever words the user and planner used.
m6.contract: Task description plus the entities and metrics it mentions.
watch: Skipping grounding entirely and retrieving on raw user phrasing

m7.carries: The same request, now unambiguous: resolved entities, agreed metric definitions, applicable rules.
m7.contract: Defined query — the terms mean what the warehouse thinks they mean.
watch: Definitions resolved but not carried through, so retrieval falls back to keywords

m8.carries: A request for the evidence this reasoning step needs, with a token budget attached.
m8.contract: Context request bounded by budget and by the acting identity.
watch: No budget passed, so retrieval optimises for recall and the context window pays for it

m9.carries: A query against systems of record, evaluated for the identity the agent acts under.
m9.contract: Data contract plus row and column policy for the acting identity.
watch: Entitlements applied at query time but lost once results enter the context window

m10.carries: Governed rows and columns, with lineage events emitted and freshness guaranteed by contract.
m10.contract: Data plus provenance; anything stale or out of contract is refused rather than returned quietly.
watch: Stale sources answering confidently because freshness is not enforced
Lineage dropped, so an incorrect answer cannot be traced

m11.carries: A recall request scoped to this tenant and this user.
m11.contract: Tenant-partitioned lookup; no cross-tenant reads under any circumstances.
watch: Shared stores with a careless key allowing cross-tenant recall

m12.carries: Prior episodes, learned facts and the procedures this organisation follows.
m12.contract: Recall with provenance per fact, so a remembered claim can be checked.
watch: Recall that is confident and wrong, because nothing scores whether a memory is still true
Memory poisoning surviving indefinitely because nothing expires

m13.carries: The assembled context package: evidence, citations, tool definitions, inside the token budget.
watch: Budget exceeded and silently truncated in the middle, where models attend least
Citations dropped during compaction, making the answer unverifiable

m14.carries: The reasoning request — sent through the gateway rather than direct to a provider.
m14.contract: OpenAI-compatible call; no direct provider access from inside the loop.
watch: Direct calls that bypass the gateway, erasing quota, cost and policy at once

m15.carries: The call, routed to a model tier, served from cache where possible, and metered.
m15.contract: Routing decision plus a cost record keyed to the trace.
watch: Cache keys that omit tenant, leaking one tenant's answer to another

m16.carries: The prompt and context, to a version-pinned model.
m16.contract: Pinned model version with a documented deprecation date.
watch: Unpinned versions changing behaviour silently between releases

m17.contract: Structured output against the declared schema.
watch: Prose returned where a schema was expected, then parsed with a regular expression

m18.carries: A structured proposal for the next action — which tool, which arguments, with what confidence.
m18.contract: Schema-valid structured output, validated before it is scored.
watch: Schema validity assumed rather than checked
Confidence taken from the model's own words rather than measured

watch: The gate placed after execution, which makes it a log rather than a control

m20.carries: An approval request, with the action and the evidence behind it, paused at a durable checkpoint.
m20.contract: The task waits without holding resources and resumes from the snapshot.

Approval fatigue from too many low-stakes interruptions

m21.carries: The human decision, recorded against the trace with the approver identity.
m21.contract: Decision written to the audit trail before execution resumes.
watch: Resumption that replays side effects already executed before the pause

watch: Approval granted for a class of actions rather than this action

Write calls without idempotency keys, so a retry duplicates the effect

m24.contract: Default-deny egress, ephemeral filesystem, root dropped, no host secrets inside.

watch: Drift unmonitored because these models sit outside agent telemetry

m30.carries: The result, an artifact, or a handle to a long-running task.
m30.contract: Typed response; long-running work returns a task handle rather than blocking.
watch: Peer agent output trusted as internal data rather than screened as external input

m34.contract: Final output with the termination reason attached.
watch: Partial results presented as complete because the stop reason was dropped

Refusals presented as errors, teaching users to route around the control

Surfaces regulation as knowledge the agent must reason about
S5.contract: An unambiguous, defined query — the same words meaning the same thing as they do in the warehouse.
watch: Semantic drift between teams, so a correct-looking answer uses the wrong definition
Regulation held as prose that nothing downstream can act on

S6A.title: Data Integration & Provenance
S6A.role: Supplies the governed corpus retrieval draws on, with entitlements and lineage attached to every row it returns.
does: Serves systems of record through contracts with freshness and quality guarantees
Enforces row and column security for the identity the agent acts under
Emits lineage so any answer can be traced to its source
S6A.contract: Governed data with entitlements applied and lineage events emitted.
watch: The agent inheriting broader entitlements than its human
PII copied into a vector index where deletion obligations cannot be met

S6B.title: Memory & State — recall
S6B.role: Contributes what the system already knew: earlier episodes, durable facts about this user or domain, and the procedures this organisation follows.
does: Recalls episodic memory of prior interactions
Supplies semantic memory — durable learned facts
Supplies procedural memory — how this organisation does this task
S6B.contract: Tenant-partitioned recall, with provenance for each remembered fact.
watch: Memory poisoning: one hostile fact written once and trusted indefinitely
A wrong memory producing the same error repeatedly, with growing confidence

S6.title: Retrieval & Context Engineering
S6.role: Assembles the smallest sufficient context for this step: hybrid search, reranking, pruning and compaction, inside a hard token budget.
does: Runs hybrid retrieval and reranks the candidates
Prunes and compacts so the context stays inside budget
Retrieves relevant tool definitions rather than loading every tool
S6.contract: A context package within the token budget, with citations attached.
watch: Context bloat and lost-in-the-middle: more context, worse answers, higher cost
Retrieved content acting as instructions — this is untrusted input, not fact

S7.title: Model & Inference
S7.role: Runs the reasoning step on a served, version-pinned model and returns a structured proposal for what to do next.
does: Serves the chosen model tier with batching and cache reuse
Produces structured output against a schema, not free prose
Falls back to another provider or an open-weight model when one degrades
S7.contract: Context in, a schema-valid next action out, with token counts attached.
watch: Unpinned versions changing behaviour silently between releases
Structured output assumed rather than validated

CORE.title: Models — the core capability
CORE.role: The generative and representational capability itself: the thing the sixteen harnesses exist to make grounded, permitted, observable and affordable.
does: Language and vision-language reasoning
Speech recognition and synthesis for voice channels
Embeddings and reranking that make retrieval work
CORE.contract: Weights and an API. Everything that makes it enterprise-grade lives outside this box.
watch: Treating model capability as the whole system: a better model does not fix a missing harness
Model choice made once and never re-measured

S8.title: Governance — approval gate
S8.role: Decides, per action, how much autonomy is permitted: proceed, require a human, or refuse. This is where policy stops being a document.
does: Scores the proposed action on impact, reversibility, data sensitivity, regulation and confidence
Lets reversible, low-impact actions run unattended and fully logged
Interrupts irreversible, financial or regulated actions for human approval at a durable checkpoint
Refuses anything outside the policy envelope outright
S8.contract: Policy-as-code evaluated per action, with the decision recorded on the trace.
watch: Approval theatre: reviewers without enough context to disagree
Gate placed after execution, which makes it a log rather than a control

S9.title: Tool, Skill & Sandbox
S9.role: Where the system actually does something: a typed tool call executed under a scoped identity, inside isolation appropriate to its blast radius.
does: Executes typed tool contracts with validated arguments
Separates read authority from write authority explicitly
Runs generated code in a microVM, application kernel or Wasm sandbox
Attaches an idempotency key to every side-effecting call
S9.contract: Typed call in, typed result or typed error out; no ambient credentials inside the sandbox.
watch: Excessive agency: broad write scopes granted for convenience
Third-party skills trusted unsigned and unscanned
Retries repeating a side effect because idempotency was never designed in

S9A.title: Protocol & Interoperability
S9A.role: Carries the call across the boundary on a standard contract, so the framework on either side can be replaced without renegotiating the integration.
does: MCP for tools, resources and data servers
A2A for delegating a task to a peer agent, with its own lifecycle
OpenAPI and AsyncAPI for the rest of the estate
S9A.contract: MCP or A2A message with a declared schema and a versioned server identity.
watch: Tool poisoning, rug-pulls and shadowing from third-party servers
Version skew as the MCP stateless core lands and deprecated features are removed

S9B.title: ML & Decision Intelligence
S9B.role: The cheaper specialist. Classifiers, rerankers, forecasts and optimisers exposed as tools, often better than a language model at the same decision.
does: Classifies, scores and routes at a fraction of the cost and latency
Detects anomalies and forecasts where the answer is a number, not prose
Solves constrained problems where the answer is a plan
S9B.contract: A tool contract like any other, with its own accuracy and drift monitoring.
watch: A language model used where a small classifier is faster, cheaper and more accurate
Drift unmonitored because these models sit outside agent telemetry

EXT.title: Systems of record & peer agents
EXT.role: The world outside the harness: databases, SaaS platforms, transactional APIs, devices, and agents belonging to other teams or organisations.
does: Accepts reads and writes under the agent's scoped identity
Returns results, artifacts or long-running task handles
Applies its own authorisation, which should be the second line of defence, not the first
EXT.contract: Whatever the system already enforces — the agent gets no special privileges.
watch: Blast radius assessed on the tool rather than on the system it touches
Peer agents trusted as if they were internal components (OWASP ASI07)

S10.title: Memory & State — write-back
S10.role: Decides what this task is allowed to leave behind: what was learned, for how long, in what form, and for which tenant.
does: Applies the write policy — what earns persistence at all
Sets TTL and retention, and redacts before storing
Partitions strictly by tenant and records provenance for each fact
S10.contract: A deliberate write, or no write. Silence is a valid outcome.
watch: Unbounded growth degrading recall precision and inflating cost
Facts persisted that cannot later be found and erased on request

S11.title: Guardrails — post-call
S11.role: The last check before anything is said or shown: does the output match its schema, its policy and its audience.
does: Validates output against the declared schema before anything acts on it
Applies policy classifiers and redacts what must not leave
Blocks and routes to a fallback rather than emitting something unsafe
S11.contract: Schema-valid, policy-clean output, or a controlled failure.
watch: Validation applied to the final message only, while intermediate steps already acted
Silent redaction that leaves the user with a misleading answer

E1.title: AI Gateway — egress
E1.role: Meters what the task consumed and attributes it before the response leaves, which is what makes cost per task a real number rather than an invoice surprise.
does: Counts tokens across every model call in the task
Charges the tenant and decrements the budget
Emits the cost record that FinOps and chargeback depend on
E1.contract: A cost record keyed to the same trace ID as the work it paid for.
watch: Cost measured per call rather than per successful task, hiding the real unit economics
Budget checked at ingress only, so an expensive loop is discovered too late

E2.title: Experience — delivery
E2.role: Delivers the result in a form the user can judge: streamed, attributed, and honest about what was uncertain or refused.
does: Streams the result rather than making the user wait in silence
Shows provenance — what this was based on
States clearly when something was refused, redacted or left uncertain
E2.contract: An answer plus the evidence needed to calibrate trust in it.
watch: Provenance hidden, so users cannot tell a grounded answer from a fluent one
Refusals presented as errors, teaching users to route around the control

A15.title: Observability & FinOps
A15.role: Records every hop so the whole task can be reconstructed later: spans, correlation IDs, the acting identity, the policy decision, and the cost.
does: Emits OpenTelemetry GenAI spans for model calls, tools, retrieval and memory
Propagates trace, thread and task IDs across every handoff and approval wait
Meters tokens and attributes cost per tenant and per task
A15.contract: A trace complete enough to replay the task without access to the original request.
watch: Classic APM blindness to the failures that matter: loops, silent quality decay, hallucinated queries
Logs that cannot distinguish agent activity from human activity

A16.title: Evaluation & Assurance
A16.role: Turns traces into judgements: graded at five scopes, repeated N times, and attacked deliberately before anything is promoted.
does: Grades component, agent, trajectory, system and trust scopes
Runs the same scenario repeatedly and reports variance, not just a median
Runs adversarial campaigns and publishes attack success rate with the judge configuration
Converts production incidents into permanent regression cases
A16.contract: Evidence, with its methodology attached, that a release gate can act on.
watch: Single-run scores treated as proof
Evaluation awareness inflating measured safety
Judges never calibrated against human graders

A14.title: AgentOps closed loop
A14.role: Closes the loop: diagnose what actually failed, change the right artefact, gate the change on evidence, deploy it, and watch it again.
does: Locates the failure — prompt, model, retrieval, memory, routing, tool, policy or infrastructure
Versions the change in a registry alongside agents, prompts, tools and policies
Gates promotion on regression, security and cost thresholds
Deploys by canary or shadow, with rollback ready
A14.contract: No change reaches production without evidence and a way back.
watch: Feedback captured but never reaching a model or prompt change
Shadow agents outside any registry, so changes cannot be governed at all

H1.title: Infrastructure & Runtime
H1.role: Hosts every harness in this diagram. Drawn once with a single connector, but it sits under all of them.
does: Kubernetes across public and private cloud, with a private path for regulated work
GPU scheduling and quota so accelerators are not idle
Storage, queues, service mesh, secrets and network policy
High availability and tested disaster recovery
H1.contract: Capacity, isolation and resilience, available without a ticket.
watch: GPU utilisation stuck at a quarter of capacity without quota and gang scheduling
Disaster recovery documented but never rehearsed

e1.carries: The task itself, plus the identity and entitlements of whoever is asking.
e1.contract: Authenticated channel session or API credential.
watch: Under-specified intent with no path to ask a clarifying question
Service-account identity that erases whose entitlements apply

e2.carries: The normalised request with session and tenant context attached.
e2.contract: Internal request envelope: tenant, session, channel, modality.
watch: Tenant inferred from the session rather than asserted explicitly

e3.carries: The request, on its way to be screened before any tokens are spent.
e3.contract: Synchronous guardrail call at the gateway edge, fail-closed.
watch: Fail-open behaviour when the guardrail service is slow or unavailable
Screening treated as sufficient because it happened at the edge

e4.carries: A cleared request plus a short-lived, narrowly scoped credential for the agent that will act.
e4.contract: Just-in-time credential bound to this task and this trace ID.
watch: Long-lived credentials issued because short-lived ones were inconvenient
Scope granted for the whole session rather than the specific task

e5.carries: The planned sub-task, in whatever words the user and planner used.
e5.contract: Task description plus the entities and metrics it mentions.
watch: Skipping grounding entirely and retrieving on raw user phrasing

e6.carries: The same request, now unambiguous: resolved entities, agreed metric definitions, applicable rules.
e6.contract: Defined query — the terms mean what the warehouse thinks they mean.
watch: Definitions resolved but not carried through, so retrieval falls back to keywords

e7.carries: Governed rows and columns from systems of record, filtered to what this identity may see, with lineage attached.
e7.contract: Data contract plus row and column policy evaluated for the acting identity.
watch: Entitlements applied at query time but lost once results enter the context window
Stale sources answering confidently because freshness is not enforced

e8.carries: Prior episodes, learned facts and procedures relevant to this task.
e8.contract: Tenant-partitioned recall with provenance per fact.
watch: Recall that is confident and wrong, because nothing scores whether a memory is still true
Cross-tenant recall from a shared store with a careless key

e9.carries: The assembled context package: evidence, citations, tool definitions, all inside the token budget.
watch: Budget exceeded and silently truncated in the middle, where models attend least
Citations dropped during compaction, making the answer unverifiable

e10.carries: Every model call in the task, routed, cached and metered on the way through.
e10.contract: OpenAI-compatible call through the gateway; no direct provider access from the loop.
watch: Direct provider calls bypassing the gateway, which erases quota, cost and policy at once

e11.carries: The reasoning capability itself — weights served behind the inference harness.
e11.contract: Version-pinned model with a documented deprecation date.
watch: Treating the model as the system: capability without a harness is a demo, not a product

e12.carries: A structured proposal for the next action — which tool, which arguments, with what confidence.
e12.contract: Schema-valid structured output; never free prose parsed with a regex.
watch: Schema validity assumed rather than checked before the action is scored
Confidence taken from the model's own words rather than measured

e13.carries: Permission to execute, either because the action is reversible and low impact, or because a human approved it.
e13.contract: Recorded policy decision carried on the trace with the approver identity.
watch: Approval granted for a class of actions rather than this action
Resumption that replays side effects already executed before the pause

e14.carries: An approval request surfaced to a human, with enough context to disagree.
e14.contract: Durable checkpoint: the task waits without holding resources, and resumes from the snapshot.
watch: Approval fatigue from too many low-stakes interruptions
A reviewer shown the action but not the evidence behind it

e15.carries: Classifier scores, rerankings and forecasts, called as ordinary tools.
e15.contract: Tool contract with its own accuracy and drift monitoring.
watch: The LLM path used for a repeated decision a small model already answers better

e16.carries: A typed tool call with validated arguments and an idempotency key.
e16.contract: Typed contract with declared inputs, outputs and error semantics.
watch: Arguments validated in the model's own output only, not at the tool boundary
Write calls without idempotency keys, so a retry duplicates the effect

e17.carries: The call out to the real world and the result back: MCP to systems and data, A2A to peer agents.
e17.contract: MCP request or A2A task; peer agents negotiate through agent cards and a task lifecycle.
watch: Third-party MCP servers unsigned, unscanned and unpinned
Peer agent output trusted as internal data rather than screened as external input

e18.carries: The result of the action, plus whatever the system now knows that it did not before.
e18.contract: Structured result appended to durable state, then re-planned against.
watch: Looping without progress because nothing measures whether the result advanced the task
Budget consumed by iterations that never converge

e19.carries: The facts, episodes or procedures this task earned the right to persist.
e19.contract: Write policy decision, with TTL and redaction applied before storage.
watch: Persisting everything by default, which degrades recall and creates retention liability

e20.carries: The completed result, or the partial result plus the reason the loop stopped.
e20.contract: Final output with the termination reason attached.
watch: Partial results presented as complete because the stop reason was dropped

e21.carries: Output that has passed schema and policy validation and been redacted where required.
e21.contract: Schema-valid, policy-clean payload, or a controlled failure path.
watch: Redaction that changes the meaning without telling the reader

e22.carries: The response, with its token cost counted and charged to the tenant.
e22.contract: Cost record keyed to the same trace ID as the work.
watch: Cost aggregated per call rather than per successful task

e23.carries: The answer, streamed, with provenance and any refusals or uncertainties stated plainly.
e23.contract: Streamed response plus the evidence to calibrate trust in it.
watch: Fluency mistaken for grounding because provenance was not shown

e24.carries: A span for every hop — model call, retrieval, memory access, tool execution, policy decision — carrying trace, thread and task IDs, the acting identity and the cost.
e24.contract: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions; correlation IDs survive queues, handoffs and approval waits.
watch: Correlation broken at an asynchronous boundary, which makes replay impossible
Instrumentation retrofitted after launch, which is the most expensive omission in this whole composition

e25.carries: Production traces converted into evaluation cases — especially the ones that failed.
e25.contract: Every incident becomes a permanent regression case.
watch: Incidents closed without a test, so the same failure returns

e26.carries: Evidence a release gate can act on: pass rates by scope, variance across runs, attack success rate, cost per successful task.
e26.contract: Scores published together with the harness and judge configuration that produced them.
watch: A single passing run treated as proof
Judges never calibrated against human graders on the cases that matter

e27.carries: Approved changes — versioned agents, prompts, models, tools and policies — deployed by canary or shadow with rollback ready.
e27.contract: Registry-tracked change with an owner and a way back.
watch: Changes applied straight to production because the canary path was never built

e28.carries: Policy authored in governance, compiled into the rules guardrails actually enforce.
e28.contract: Policy-as-code, versioned and deployed like any other artefact.
watch: Written standard and deployed rules drifting apart, which makes the policy decorative

e29.carries: Compute, isolation and resilience for every harness in this diagram. Drawn once as a single connector, but it applies to all of them.
e29.contract: Scheduled capacity with tenancy, secrets and network policy attached.
watch: Model serving and the gateway buried inside the platform, which makes changing either one a platform migration
